showcaseTabs.name: Road Corridor Preparation
showcaseTabs.title: Road Corridor Preparation
showcaseTabs.desc:
Road-corridor preparation may include clearing loose material, removing unsuitable surface material and preparing the defined pavement area for earthwork and subsequent road layers.

Existing utilities, drainage structures, chambers, buildings, access routes and operating areas should be identified before excavation or disturbance begins.

The scope on this page is limited to earthworks required directly for the road corridor.

Bulk site excavation, foundation excavation and general sitewide earthworks remain under Civil Works.

Excavation, Cutting and Formation
Road formation may require cutting high areas, removing unsuitable material, controlled filling and shaping the corridor to the approved line and level.

Excavated material should be assessed for reuse, stockpiling or disposal according to the project specification.

The completed formation should provide a stable and correctly shaped platform for the pavement layers above.

Where excavation extends beyond the road corridor into general site development, that work remains part of the Civil Works scope.

Filling and Subgrade Preparation
The subgrade supports the entire pavement structure.

Approved fill should be placed in controlled layers and compacted according to the required moisture condition, layer thickness and testing criteria.

Weak areas, pumping zones or unsuitable material should be identified before pavement layers are placed.

Normal filling and compaction associated with road formation remain part of Road Construction.

Where the project requires engineered treatment such as specialist soil stabilization, vibro compaction, deep soil mixing or grouting, the work is handled separately under Ground Improvement Services.

Aggregate Subbase
Subbase helps distribute pavement loads and provides a stable layer for further construction.

The approved aggregate should be checked for grading, contamination and general condition before placement.

Construction controls may include:

approved material source
layer thickness
moisture condition
spreading
level control
compaction
density testing
finished-surface acceptance
The completed layer should be inspected before the next pavement layer begins.

Aggregate Base Course
Base course provides the principal granular support beneath the asphalt where required by the approved pavement design.

Material should be spread evenly, shaped to the required profile and compacted to the specified density.

Segregation, contamination, rutting or incorrect layer thickness should be corrected before asphalt construction begins.

Prime Coat and Tack Coat Applications
Prime coat may be applied to an approved granular surface before asphalt placement where required by the pavement specification.

Tack coat may be used between asphalt layers or between existing and new pavement to support proper bonding.

Before application, the surface should be clean and free from loose dust, mud, standing water, oil and construction debris.

Application rate, coverage and curing requirements should follow the approved project specification and product requirements.

Asphalt Supply, Laying and Compaction
As an asphalt works contractor KSA projects may require for defined paving packages, BIC coordinates asphalt placement around approved mix requirements, workfront readiness, transport conditions, paving equipment, rolling sequence and inspection requirements.

Asphalt works may include:

surface preparation
delivery coordination
paving
joint preparation
layer control
rolling and compaction
edge treatment
testing
finished-surface inspection
Asphalt mix type, lift thickness, delivery temperature, laying temperature, joint preparation and compaction requirements should follow the approved project specification.

Coordination between the asphalt plant, transport vehicles, paver, rollers and inspection team helps reduce cold joints, segregation and unnecessary interruptions.

Asphalt Joints and Surface Quality
Longitudinal joints, transverse joints, paving starts, stops, edges and connections to existing pavement should be carefully prepared.

The paving sequence should minimise unnecessary joints wherever practical.

Finished asphalt may be checked for:

segregation
open texture
roller marks
surface tearing
contamination
irregular joints
poor transitions
other visible defects
Acceptance should follow the project specification and approved inspection requirements.

Road Shoulders, Edges and Tie-ins
Road works may include compacted shoulders, asphalt shoulders, edge treatment, transitions and connections to existing roads.

Finished levels should coordinate with surrounding ground and drainage so that water does not collect along pavement edges.

Tie-ins to gates, ramps, loading areas, yards and existing roads should be reviewed before final paving.

Road Reinstatement and Local Pavement Repairs
Road reinstatement may be required after utility installation, maintenance activities or modification works.

Affected areas should be reconstructed according to the approved pavement structure rather than covered with only a thin asphalt patch.

Depending on the required repair, the work may include:

cutting and removal
excavation
backfilling
subgrade preparation
aggregate layers
prime or tack coat
asphalt replacement
joint treatment
compaction
finished-level adjustment
The repaired pavement should connect properly with the surrounding surface.

faqs.q: What road construction work does BIC provide?
faqs.a: BIC has an opportunity to check out the appropriate packages of site preparation, road formation, filling, subgrade, aggregate layers, bituminous treatments, asphalt paving, shoulders, tie-ins and reinstatement.

faqs.q: Is BIC able to develop the industrial access roads in Jubail?
faqs.a: Yes. Jubail has defined industrial road packages that can be compared to the pavement design, site access, operational restrictions, quantities and schedule required.

faqs.q: Does your road work include road marking?
faqs.a: Road marking is an additional service and will only be included in the accepted scope and proposal when it is mentioned.

faqs.q: Can you repair damaged asphalt roads?
faqs.a: Yes. Repairs to the local, reconstruction of failed areas, reinstatement of the trench, an overlay and other solutions can be evaluated once the status of the pavement and the necessary method of repair are determined.

faqs.q: Who provides the asphalt mix design?
faqs.a: The process of approval should go through the project in order to give the approved mix design and acceptance criteria. When they are mentioned in the contract, responsibility in mix development is not a part of it.

faqs.q: Do you provide testing for compaction and asphalt works?
faqs.a: The coordination of the required testing can happen based on the accepted inspection plan. The proposal ought to specify testing to be done by BIC, the client or the consultant or by an appointed lab.

faqs.q: Is it feasible to pave over an existing road?
faqs.a: The overlay can only be appropriate after the current pavement condition, levels, drainage and treatment needed is checked. The failed regions might require to be removed and rebuilt initially.

faqs.q: How is the road construction schedule determined?
faqs.a: The schedule is based on quantities, work fronts, material approvals, haulage distances, utilities, inspection and continuity of paving, weather and traffic limitations.

faqs.q: Do the quotation include equipment and materials?
faqs.a: They will be mentioned only when explicit. The proposal identifies responsibility for fill, aggregate, asphalt, bituminous products, equipment, testing and temporary arrangements.

faqs.q: What should we send for a road construction quotation?
faqs.a: Submit the road plan, pavement section, quantities, specifications, location, dates needed, information about the state of existing condition and responsibility table.

showcaseTabs.title: Road and Pavement Marking Applications
showcaseTabs.desc:
Centre Lines, Lane Lines and Edge Lines
Road lines can be used to separate traffic movements, define lanes, guide vehicles and identify pavement edges.

The approved layout should define the required width, colour, pattern and location of each line.

Curves, junctions and narrow access roads require careful setting-out so that alignment and spacing remain consistent.

Directional Arrows and Pavement Symbols
Directional arrows and approved pavement symbols can communicate movement instructions, stopping locations, speed information and other facility requirements.

Templates, dimensions, orientation and positioning should follow the issued marking schedule.

BIC applies the approved symbols but does not determine traffic-control requirements unless that design responsibility is specifically included.

Stop Lines and Junction Markings
Access points and intersections may require stop lines, give-way markings, turning directions and other approved junction markings.

Their location should coordinate with gates, barriers, pedestrian crossings, visibility and existing traffic arrangements.

Pedestrian Crossings and Walkways
Industrial plants, commercial properties, warehouses and project sites may require marked pedestrian routes between parking areas, buildings, gates and operating areas.

Crossings and walkways should follow the approved facility layout and coordinate with kerbs, ramps and physical barriers.

Parking Bays and Numbering
Parking areas may include standard bays, visitor spaces, fleet parking, accessible spaces, loading areas and numbered locations.

Bay size, aisle arrangement, reserved spaces and numbering should be confirmed before marking begins.

Existing parking areas can be completed in phases where access needs to remain available.

Loading and Logistics Area Markings
Warehouses and logistics yards may require loading bays, trailer positions, forklift routes, staging zones and other operational markings.

BIC installs the approved layout according to the required dimensions and marking system.

Operational traffic design, lifting zones and safety separation distances remain the responsibility of the authorised project or facility team.

Kerb and Hazard Markings
Kerbs, islands, low obstacles and designated hazard areas may require contrasting or colour-coded markings.

The required colours, locations and extent should be defined in the project information before application.

Warehouse and Internal Floor Markings
Suitable internal areas may require aisle markings, pedestrian routes, storage boundaries, keep-clear zones and other floor markings.

Material selection should consider the existing floor surface, indoor conditions, expected traffic and specified performance requirements.

Specialist floor-coating systems and major floor repairs remain separate from the normal road marking scope.

New surfaces should meet the preparation or curing requirements of the selected marking material before application.

Existing surfaces should be checked for:

Worn markings can be renewed where the existing pavement remains suitable.

Where the road requires asphalt resurfacing, structural pavement repair or major reconstruction, that work should be completed under Road Construction & Asphalt Works before marking begins.

Road Marking Materials
The appropriate marking material depends on the approved specification, pavement type, traffic conditions, required finish and application method.

Depending on project requirements, marking systems may include approved liquid-applied materials, thermoplastic systems, preformed markings or other specified products.

Material approval should confirm relevant requirements such as:

colour
thickness
finish
reflective properties where required
application requirements
drying or curing conditions
product documentation
BIC applies the approved system and does not substitute another material without the required project approval.

Surface Preparation
Surface preparation is important for marking adhesion and appearance.

The work area should be clean, dry and suitable for the selected system.

Depending on the existing surface, preparation may include sweeping, air cleaning, approved washing, degreasing or local removal of loose material.

Oil, grease, dust, sand, loose aggregate and other contamination should be removed before marking begins.

Where the pavement itself is damaged, the underlying repair should be completed before the marking operation.

Setting-Out and Marking Application
Markings should be positioned according to approved references.

Depending on the layout, references may include pavement edges, road centre lines, kerbs, parking boundaries, building grids or project-issued survey information.

Setting-out checks may confirm:

alignment

**Soil Stabilization Services Saudi Arabia**
Soil stabilization services Saudi Arabia projects require may involve controlled treatment of suitable in-situ soil using approved binders or other specified materials.

The objective may be to improve strength, reduce deformation, enhance working conditions or achieve another defined engineering requirement.

Depending on the approved method, soil stabilization work can include:

2. distribution of approved binder
3. controlled mixing
4. treatment to the specified depth
5. moisture management
6. shaping and finishing
7. curing
8. sampling and testing support
Binder type, dosage, treatment depth, mixing requirements and acceptance criteria should be defined by the approved design.

Conventional excavation, general filling and normal site compaction that do not form part of an engineered treatment method are carried out as separate civil works.

Vibro compaction may be specified where suitable loose granular soils require densification at depth.

As a vibro compaction contractor KSA projects can appoint for approved treatment packages, BIC coordinates specialist equipment access, treatment-point locations, sequencing, backfill requirements where applicable, production records and verification activities.

The approved design should establish:

1. treatment pattern
2. point spacing
3. treatment depth
4. equipment parameters
5. backfill requirements
6. completion criteria
7. verification testing
Ground response is monitored against the approved method rather than treatment being judged solely by equipment penetration.

**Deep Soil Mixing Saudi Arabia**
Deep soil mixing Saudi Arabia projects may require where soft or unsuitable ground needs treatment to improve strength, reduce compressibility or achieve other specified geotechnical performance.

The method involves controlled mixing of in-situ soil with an approved binder system using specialist equipment.

Depending on the project, the treatment design may specify:

1. column or panel geometry
2. treatment depth
3. element diameter
4. overlap
5. binder composition
6. dosage
7. mixing parameters
8. production sequence
9. trial requirements

BIC carries out the approved execution method and maintains treatment records required for verification and handover.

1. compaction grouting
2. permeation grouting
3. fissure grouting
4. controlled void filling
5. localised treatment
Execution can include drilling coordination, packer installation, grout preparation, staged injection and monitoring of pressure and volume.

The approved method should identify injection locations, treatment sequence, pressure limits, volume limits, termination criteria and any movement-monitoring requirements.

When grouting is carried out close to existing foundations, pipelines, chambers or operating structures, the project may also require defined trigger levels and monitoring controls.

Site preparation may include clearing loose or unsuitable material, initial grading, preparing approved access routes, establishing working areas and coordinating temporary site requirements.

Existing utilities, structures, roads, drainage features and operating areas should be identified before disturbance begins.

Working platforms, haul routes and stockpile locations should be planned according to the equipment required, site restrictions and the condition of the ground.

Excavation around existing utilities, foundations or operating facilities may require utility detection, trial pits, controlled digging, hand excavation, shoring, monitoring or other approved precautions.

All work should follow the applicable excavation permit, method statement and project safety requirements.

As an excavation and backfilling contractor KSA project packages may engage for defined earthwork requirements, BIC can support foundation excavations, trenches, utility routes and general site earthworks.

Backfilling should be carried out using materials that meet the approved project specification.

The material type, moisture condition, layer thickness, placement method, compaction equipment and testing frequency should be established before filling begins.

Unsuitable excavated material should not be reused simply because it is available on site.

Where imported fill, selected material or another specified material is required, sourcing, approval, placement and testing should follow the project requirements.

Conventional excavation, filling and compaction remain within this Civil Works scope. Specialist treatment of weak or unsuitable ground using techniques such as soil stabilisation, vibro compaction, deep soil mixing or specialist grouting is covered separately under Ground Improvement Services.

Foundation and Equipment Base Works
Foundation construction may include excavation, formation preparation, blinding concrete, reinforcement, formwork, embedded items, anchor bolts, concrete placement, curing and finishing.

Foundations for buildings, equipment, structures and supports can have different loading, tolerance, vibration and interface requirements. The approved structural drawings and inspection requirements should therefore be confirmed before construction.

Reinforcement and Embedded Items

Before concrete placement, inspection may include reinforcement grade, diameter, spacing, laps, cover and general fixing condition.

Anchor bolts, sleeves, inserts, conduits, plates, waterstops and similar embedded items should be coordinated before the pour because changes after concrete has hardened may be difficult or unacceptable.

Formwork and Concrete Finishing
Formwork should maintain the required dimensions, line, level and finish while safely resisting the loads generated during concrete placement.

Finished concrete may require formed, trowelled, brushed or other approved finishes depending on the intended application.

Slopes, edges, chamfers, joints and tolerances should be inspected so that the completed work is suitable for the next construction activity.

The civil scope should clearly identify the boundary between concrete and foundation works and the associated fabrication or structural-steel package.

The installation of pipes, cables or specialist systems should be identified separately where it falls outside the agreed civil scope.

Correct levels and gradients are especially important for drainage works. Survey and inspection checks should therefore be completed at the required stages before the work is covered.

Standalone topographic surveys, underground utility surveys, GNSS surveys and formal as-built survey services remain under Land Survey Services.

Civil repair works may include removal of damaged concrete, preparation of the repair area, treatment of reinforcement, placement of approved repair materials and reinstatement of the completed surface.

The repair method should be selected according to the nature and cause of the defect rather than simply covering visible damage.

Excavation Support and Dewatering
Excavation stability can be affected by depth, soil condition, groundwater, adjacent loads, surrounding structures and the expected duration of the excavation.

Depending on the approved method, excavations may require sloping, benching, shoring or another suitable support arrangement.

Where water enters the excavation, pumping and dewatering arrangements should consider discharge locations, standby capacity and any applicable environmental controls.

weather conditions

Safety and Environmental Controls
Civil work may involve excavation, heavy equipment, moving vehicles, lifting activities, concrete placement, temporary works, dust, noise and work near existing facilities.

showcaseTabs.title: Choosing the Right Equipment for the Job
showcaseTabs.desc:
Such a choice of equipment by model name may cause unnecessary issues. A machine that works well in a particular environment might not be applicable in another site where there is a limited access, soft ground, lack of clearance or variant production requirements. Project teams ought to take into consideration the following before asking to be quoted:

- The precise work that the equipment should carry out.
- Capacity, reach, lifting height, bucket size or load rating needed.
- Ground condition, working space available and access route.
- Hours of operation per day and total hours that should be rented.
- Fuel, power connection or other site-support considerations.
- The need or requirement of an experienced operator or driver.
- Site induction, permit, safety documentation or client approval documentation.

Early provision of such details assists in determining an option that would be practical and be able to plan well on the industrial equipment rental Saudi Arabia projects.

faqs.q: What information is needed for an equipment rental quotation?
faqs.a: Provide the type of equipment, site location, type of work, when the equipment is required to start and how long it is needed, the capacity needed and the working hours and operator requirement. Access or approval requirements of the site should also be noted.

faqs.q: How do I know which equipment model or capacity is suitable?
faqs.a: Indicate the task and conditions of operation instead of just picking a model name. Load, reach, terrain, access, working height, production target and available space will assist in making a more realistic choice.

faqs.q: Is it possible to extend the rental period after the equipment has arrived on site?
faqs.a: Extension can be done in case it is requested prior to the off-hire date agreed upon, based on the equipment commitments, availability and revised commercial confirmation.

faqs.q: Are fuel and consumables included in the rental?
faqs.a: Depending on the equipment and rental agreement, inclusions are different. Quotation should clearly confirm fuel, consumable, operators accommodation, transportation and other site related responsibilities.

faqs.q: How early should I request equipment for a project?
